newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour used brand strategy to win - ad execs.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour used brand strategy to win - ad execs.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who led his Labour party to victory in the recent election by promoting the image "New Labour," is a classic example of how good marketing sells a brand, advertising executives said.
Similar to the way consumer goods companies market cereal, the Labour Party researched what the public wanted and delivered the product demanded.
"Tony Blair ... changed the product, he changed the price, he changed the package," Graham Hinton, chairman of advertising agency Bates, Dorland, part of Cordiant Plc, said in a recent speech.
"Most important, he managed (the Labour party) like a brand," Hinton said.
"Labour reached out over the heads of pundits and created a new relationship with voters," he added.
Hugh Burkitt, chairman of ad agency Court, Burkitt & Co., noted that Labour followed the classic path of good marketing: It researched its market to determine what voters wanted.
"Good advertising is never one-way," Burkitt told Reuters. "It's always based on what your target audience thinks."

By using focus groups, Labour determined how it needed to reposition itself to meet voters' desires. From party policies to sartorial style, Labour used classic brand marketing strategy to develop and sell a political product the British electorate wanted.

Labour, which had been out of power for 18 years when it triumphed over Conservative Prime Minister John Major last month, worked at many levels over the years leading up to the 1997 general election to develop the right product, Burkitt said.

Labour examined the mood of the electorate and repositioned itself toward the centre, moving away from its leftist heritage. The party literally put itself in a new suit of clothes by getting leaders to wear dark suits and ties, replacing the rumpled look that had characterised many in the party, Burkitt said.
Labour even adopted what Bates Dorland's Hinton called "the oldest trick in the book": renaming itself New Labour, similar to the way consumer goods promote their new versions, such as New Coke.
"They redesigned the product and stuck with it," Hinton told Reuters.
"The Tories fell into the trap, because they called it New Labour," Hinton added.

Although both Labour and the Conservatives were criticised throughout the campaign for lacklustre advertising, advertising executives said Labour's solid marketing strategy made its advertising secondary.
"All they had to do was stay out of trouble," said Hinton.
"The biggest indication that the brand job had been done prior to the election is the Labour team did not spend its time during the election writing ads," Hinton said.
In addition, Labour used direct-mail advertising in a highly effective manner, targeting swing voters with key mailings.

One Labour party mailing featured a credit-card-sized card with Tony Blair's photo on one side and the party's five top policies listed on the other one side, topped by the message "Keep this card and see that we keep our promises."
